title: Big Corp, Startup or Outsourcing: Same Title, Different Job
summary: The same engineering title means three different jobs in a big corp, a startup and an outsourcing shop. Where work comes from, who decides, and how to pick a fit.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Three engineers, same title: Senior Software Engineer. The first spends Tuesday morning getting four teams to agree on an API contract, then waits two days for a security review. The second writes a feature, asks a teammate to look it over and deploys it before lunch. The third is on a late call with a client in another time zone, explaining why one "small" change request adds two weeks.

None of them is better at the job. They work in different places, and the place shapes the job more than the title does. It decides where your tasks come from, who gets to say yes, how much process sits between you and production, and what gets you promoted.

I've worked in all three: outsourcing at Splus Software, a B2B product startup at PrimeData, and big tech on Zalo PC at VNG. This post is the map I'd hand a friend before a move like that. It won't crown a winner. It compares the three on the things that change your actual day, so you can read the place you're in (or about to join) and set fair expectations. Each world then gets its own deep dive later in the series.

Three kinds of company, roughly

These are archetypes. Most real companies are a mix, and plenty change type as they grow. The three points are still clear enough to reason about:

TypeWhat it isWho pays, and for what
Big corp / enterpriseA large product or platform company: hundreds or thousands of people, many teams, processes that have been around for years.Customers pay for the product. You're a specialist in a big system built for scale and reliability.
StartupA young product company still working out what sells. Steve Blank's definition is the useful one: "an organization formed to search for a repeatable and scalable business model" (What's a Startup? First Principles).Investors and early customers are paying for how fast the team learns. You're a generalist who trades polish for momentum.
Outsourcing / servicesAn agency, consultancy or software house that builds software for other companies under contract.A client pays for delivery against an agreed scope. You build someone else's product to an agreement.

The simplest split: a product company (big corp or startup) lives or dies by the product it owns. A services company lives or dies by its client relationships and the contracts it delivers. Big corp and startup differ mostly in size and stage. Services differs in who owns the outcome.

What actually changes day to day

Skip the stereotypes (corp is boring, startups have bean bags, outsourcing is a code factory). The real differences come down to a short list:

  • Where the work comes from: how a task lands on your plate.
  • Who decides, and how fast.
  • How heavy the process is: ceremonies, approvals, compliance.
  • How much you own: deep and narrow, or wide and shallow.
  • How you communicate: meetings, docs, async, stakeholders.
  • Pace, risk and the quality bar.
  • What gets rewarded.

Take them one at a time and the three worlds get much easier to tell apart.

Where the work comes from

In a big corp, work comes down a planning chain. Company strategy becomes org objectives (often OKRs), objectives become a roadmap, the roadmap becomes epics for your team, and epics become the stories you pick up. By the time a ticket reaches you, a lot of people have already agreed it matters. You get clarity and alignment. You also get a long distance between you and the "why", and changing direction takes a while.

In a startup, work comes from whatever moves the business this month: a founder's hunch, a customer who just churned, a competitor's launch, a number that refuses to grow. The roadmap might be a shared doc someone edited last night. You sit close to the "why" and can push on it. The catch is that priorities swing hard, and "urgent" keeps eating "important".

In outsourcing, work comes from the contract. There's a statement of work, a backlog agreed with the client and a scope that says what's included and what counts as a change request. The client owns the what. Your team owns the how and the delivery. Boundaries are clear, though you often build requirements you didn't shape, for a product strategy you only see part of.

The tell

Ask "where did this ticket come from?" In a big corp the honest answer climbs an org chart. In a startup it points at a person or a metric. In outsourcing it points at a contract and someone on the client side. That one question predicts a lot of the rest.

Who decides, and how fast

This is the difference you feel first, usually in your first week.

In a big corp, decisions are spread out and well guarded. A change may need agreement across teams, sign-off from a lead or architect, and a nod from security, legal or the platform team. Much of that is real protection: at scale, one team's shortcut becomes another team's outage. The cost is speed. What takes an afternoon in a startup can take three meetings and a design doc here.

Jeff Bezos named the trap in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. Some decisions are one-way doors, hard or impossible to undo, and they deserve slow, careful deliberation. Most are two-way doors you can walk back through, and a small group should make them quickly. His warning: "As organizations get larger, there seems to be a tendency to use the heavy-weight Type 1 decision-making process on most decisions, including many Type 2 decisions." The result, in his words, is "slowness, unthoughtful risk aversion, failure to experiment sufficiently." A habit worth stealing anywhere: before a decision joins the approval queue, ask which kind of door it is.

In a startup, decisions are cheap and local. You can often decide and ship the same day, and authority follows trust more than titles. The risk runs the other way: too little thought, so the team re-decides the same thing three times and the codebase ends up with three answers. Writing decisions down helps a lot, and a short decision log is the lightest way to start.

In outsourcing, decisions split along a line. Technical "how" calls are usually yours. Product "what" and scope calls belong to the client, and changing them means a request, a reason and sometimes a contract amendment. The skill is knowing which side of the line you're on before you act.

How heavy the process is

Every team says it "does Agile". What that looks like scales with how expensive a mistake is.

ProcessBig corpStartupOutsourcing
CeremoniesFull Scrum or a scaled framework such as SAFe, several layers, formal planningLight or improvised. "Standup" might be a Slack threadScrum shaped around the client. Their cadence usually wins
ApprovalsSeveral gates: code review, security, a change advisory boardFew. Ship and learnClient sign-off on scope, demos and acceptance
DocumentationHeavy and long-lived (audits, handovers, compliance)Minimal. The code and the founders' heads are the docsContractual. Docs are deliverables the client pays for
EstimatesUsed for capacity planning across teamsOften skipped, or roughTied to billing, so an estimate can turn into a commitment

Martin Fowler's note on fixed-price contracts explains that last row. Fixing price, time and scope all at once "requires detailed, stable, and accurate requirements," which software rarely has. His suggestion for agile teams is to fix the budget and the date, then choose the scope together as everyone learns. A lot of services teams live inside exactly that negotiation, sprint after sprint.

For what epics, stories, points and ceremonies are supposed to be, and how teams bend them, see Agile & Scrum in Practice. The point here is simpler: process weight should follow the cost of being wrong. A bank's payment platform earns its gates. A startup with no revenue running bank-grade process is paying for maturity it doesn't need yet.

How much you own

This is the one that surprises people most when they switch.

In a big corp, ownership is deep and narrow. You might own one service, one stage of a pipeline or one part of the UI, and know it inside out. Specialists handle the rest: SREs, DBAs, a design system team, a release team. You go deep and lean on others for breadth.

In a startup, ownership is wide, and shallow out of necessity. In one week you might write a backend endpoint, fix some CSS, set up a deploy, talk to a customer and argue about pricing. You own outcomes, and tickets are only how you track them. The fun part is range and impact you can see. The cost is doing things you aren't expert at yet, on a system only two people fully understand.

In outsourcing, the engagement defines what you own. On a staff augmentation contract you join the client's team and own a component like one of their engineers. On a project contract your team owns delivery end to end, until handover, when someone else inherits it. Either way you're responsible for the work and for the relationship, a kind of ownership many product engineers never practice.

A useful reframe

Swap "what will I build?" for "how wide is my circle of ownership, and who else is in it?" Deep and narrow, wide and shallow, and bounded by a contract are three different jobs that happen to share one title.

How you communicate

Melvin Conway spotted the link between org shape and software in 1968: organizations that design systems "are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations" (How Do Committees Invent?). How a place talks ends up in its code, so it's worth paying attention to.

Big corps run on written, async, long-lived communication, because the audience is large and keeps changing: design docs, RFCs, tickets that explain themselves, decisions written down so the next team can find them. You'll spend real time with stakeholders, the people your work affects who aren't on your team. There are lots of meetings, and the skill is keeping yours few and useful.

Startups run on fast, low-ceremony talk across the desk or in Slack. You can lean over and ask. The danger is that key context lives only in heads and DMs, so when the team doubles, half the knowledge goes missing. Good small teams start writing things down before that bites.

Outsourcing adds a second audience you have to serve on purpose: the client. Status updates, demos, written scope confirmations and early risk flags are core work, and they're how trust (and the next contract) gets built. Time zones make it harder and make clear async writing a must-have skill.

Pace, risk and the quality bar

There's no single quality bar. Google's SRE book puts it plainly: "We strive to make a service reliable enough, but no more reliable than it needs to be," and "100% is probably never the right reliability target" (Embracing Risk). The same chapter notes that one more increment of reliability may cost 100x more than the previous one. Each environment picks its bar from the risk it carries.

  • Big corp: slow and safe. An outage is expensive and public, so the bar is high: tests, reviews, rollbacks, observability. You optimize for not breaking what already works. Tech debt is real, and it gets managed like a portfolio.
  • Startup: fast and scrappy. Building the wrong thing perfectly can sink the company, so you trade polish for learning. Debt you take on deliberately is a tool. Debt nobody noticed is how a startup that survived year one slowly stalls.
  • Outsourcing: quality is whatever the contract and the client require, and your reputation rides on hitting it. The squeeze comes when a fixed budget meets a client who expects perfection. Managing that gap is half the job.

What gets rewarded

Each place promotes the behavior it needs. Over a few years, this is the difference that shapes you most.

RewardsBig corpStartupOutsourcing
Who stands outGets teams pointed the same way, lands cross-team projects, lowers riskOwns outcomes, ships fast, spots what matters before anyone asksKeeps commitments, keeps clients happy, brings repeat work
Career pathClear ladders, levels, calibrated promotionsFuzzy and fast: big titles early, scope that jumps overnightOften two tracks: technical depth, or client and account management
The riskFeeling like one small part of a huge machine, impact spread thinBurnout, and a role that grows faster than anyone defines itBroad skills from many projects, little depth in any one product

So which one fits you?

There's no universal answer. Fit usually follows what you want right now:

  • A big corp, if you want depth, mentors, problems at real scale, stability and a clear ladder, and you can live with slower decisions and a longer line to the customer.
  • A startup, if you want range, ownership, speed and a seat near the business, and you can handle ambiguity, some instability and doing things you're not good at yet.
  • Outsourcing, if you want many domains and clients, fast skill-broadening and you enjoy the craft of delivery and client work, and you're fine not owning one product for years.

Career stage matters too. Early on, a startup's breadth or an agency's variety teaches a lot fast, and a big corp's structured mentoring builds solid foundations. Later, the question becomes which kind of impact you want to grow. To borrow Bezos's phrase once more, none of these is a one-way door. Plenty of good engineers move through all three on purpose.

The hybrids you'll actually meet

  • Scale-ups: startups that found product-market fit and are growing fast. Startup speed runs into brand-new process, often awkwardly.
  • Labs and internal startups inside big companies: startup pace with corporate safety nets, and corporate politics attached.
  • Product-minded outsourcing: services firms that build long-term products for one client and work much like an embedded product team.
  • Staff augmentation vs project delivery: two very different outsourcing jobs. One puts you inside the client's team as an individual. The other makes your vendor team own a whole project.

When you size up a company, don't trust the label. Ask the questions from each section above and you'll place it on the map yourself in about ten minutes of interview time.

Questions for your next interview

  • "Where did the last ticket you worked on come from?"
  • "Who approves a change to a shared API, and how long does that usually take?"
  • "What happens when an estimate turns out wrong?"
  • "What did the last person promoted on this team do to get there?"
  • "If I join, what will I own by day 90?"

Each world gets a closer look in the next posts of the series: big corp, startup and outsourcing.

faqs.q: Is a big corp, a startup or outsourcing the best place to work as a software engineer?
faqs.a: None is best for everyone. A big corp gives depth, mentors, stability and a clear career ladder, at the cost of slower decisions and distance from customers. A startup gives range, ownership and speed, at the cost of stability and polish. Outsourcing gives many domains and clients and broadens your skills fast, at the cost of long-term ownership of one product. Pick for what you want right now, and remember you can move between them later.

faqs.q: What's the real difference between a product company and a services company?
faqs.a: A product company (big corp or startup) owns what it builds and lives or dies by that product. A services company builds software for other companies under contract and lives or dies by its client relationships and delivery. In practice, a product company lets you influence what gets built. In services, the client owns the what, and your team owns the how and the delivery.

faqs.q: Why is process so much heavier in big companies?
faqs.a: Because mistakes cost more at scale: one team's shortcut can become another team's outage or a compliance problem, so reviews and sign-offs earn their place. The trap is applying that heavy process to every decision. Jeff Bezos's 2015 shareholder letter warns that large organizations tend to use slow, careful decision-making even for reversible choices, which leads to slowness and too little experimentation. Process weight should follow the cost of being wrong.

faqs.q: Will I learn more at a startup or at a big company?
faqs.a: You learn different things. A startup teaches breadth fast: backend, frontend, infrastructure, product and customers, often in the same month, though depth in any one area can stay thin. A big company teaches depth and rigor: scale problems, strong fundamentals and structured mentoring, within a narrower scope. Outsourcing teaches breadth across domains plus delivery and client communication. Choose by the gap you most want to fill.

faqs.q: How can I tell what kind of company I'm interviewing with?
faqs.a: Ignore the label and ask concrete questions. Where did the last ticket come from: a roadmap, a founder or metric, or a client contract? Who approves a change to a shared API, and how long does it take? What happens when an estimate is wrong? What did the last promoted person do? What will you own by day 90? The answers place any company on the map, hybrids such as scale-ups and internal startups included.
